structure.title: Prologue and parodos · A god comes home in disguise
structure.text: Dionysus comes to his mother's city to establish the truth of her story and his claim to worship. The audience hears his identity from his own mouth before King Pentheus begins looking for a suspicious foreigner.

structure.title: First episode – fourth stasimon · An interrogation that changes direction
structure.text: Pentheus wants to know what the women are doing on the mountain. Questioning the stranger brings him no closer to control. Curiosity offers Dionysus a means of moving the king himself towards the place he wants to police.

structure.title: Exodos · News comes down the mountain
structure.text: The audience receives events outside the city through witnesses. Someone who has taken part may understand the very same scene quite differently. Recognition can be more terrible than the first report.

people.name: Pentheus
people.text: He interprets worship as disorder and women outside their households as a sexual threat. His own desire to see what he condemns leaves him particularly vulnerable to a plausible guide.

people.name: Dionysus and his worshippers
people.text: The stranger answers with disconcerting patience. His followers sing of release from labour and of a mountain alive with joy. Their pleasure belongs in the same play as the terror his power can bring.

context.title: Two groups of women
context.text: The chorus came with Dionysus from Asia. The women of Thebes have been driven from their homes to the mountain. What one group sings of as willing devotion cannot simply be assumed of the other.

notice.text: Watch who arranges another person's clothes.
notice.why: An outfit can let a spy approach unnoticed. Being dressed and inspected by the very person he means to observe also gives away a considerable measure of control.

notice.text: Compare the mountain a messenger sees with the one Pentheus imagines.
notice.why: The eyewitness describes tenderness, abundance and sudden violence. The king selects from the report what his existing suspicions equip him to hear.

opening: A new religious frenzy has drawn the women of Thebes out into the mountains, and King Pentheus intends to restore order. The stranger encouraging it seems an easy person to arrest. What Pentheus does not understand is that the god he refuses to acknowledge is present, enjoying the encounter, and attentive to the curiosity beneath his outrage. Euripides brings desire, humiliation, and divine power into a confrontation where the ruler's determination to expose other people's madness makes him increasingly available for manipulation.
